## The Country Beneath the Night

Here is a strange fact to sit with: we hold better maps of the surface of Mars than of our own planet's seafloor. More than two-thirds of Earth is ocean, and most of that ocean has never been seen by human eyes. The average depth of the sea is nearly four kilometers; if we drained the water and set Mount Everest on the floor of an average stretch, its summit would still lie five kilometers beneath where the waves used to be. We have photographed the dust of another world in crisp detail while the majority of our own planet remains dark, unvisited, and—there's no honest way around it—strange beyond our imagining.

The trouble begins two hundred meters down. That is where sunlight gives up. Red vanishes first, then orange, then yellow, until the water is not blue but something older than blue, a color with no name because no one was around to name it. Scientists call the next stretch of ocean the twilight zone, though twilight is generous. It is more like the last breath of a fire, and then not even that.

And yet the deep is not empty. Every night, the largest migration of animals on Earth takes place, and it happens vertically. Lanternfish, squid, and copepods no bigger than grains of rice rise hundreds of meters toward the surface to feed under cover of darkness, then sink again at dawn. In sheer biomass this dwarfs the wildebeest herds, the caribou, everything that walks. For decades, sonar operators noticed that the seafloor seemed to rise at dusk and fall at dawn—a phantom bottom that turned out to be alive. The greatest movement of life on this planet was hiding in plain echo, and we mistook it for the ground.

Below a thousand meters lies the midnight zone, where sunlight has never arrived, not once in four billion years. Pressure becomes the law of the place. At the bottom of the Mariana Trench, nearly eleven kilometers down, the water presses with more than a thousand times the force of the air at sea level—picture an elephant balanced on your thumbnail, then keep multiplying.

And yet: life, not merely enduring but diversifying into forms no one thought to imagine. Consider that in the deep sea, most animals make their own light. Biologists who have counted estimate that three-quarters of deep-sea species are bioluminescent, which may make glowing the most common form of communication on Earth. On land, almost nothing does it. Blue light travels farthest through water, so the deep conducts its affairs in blue: a flash here means mate; a burst there means decoy; some squid spit luminous mucus like flares to blind and mislead pursuers. The abyss is not dark the way an empty room is dark. It is dark the way a city at night is dark—signals everywhere, none of them meant for us.

The residents earn their reputations. The barreleye fish has a transparent skull and tubular eyes that swivel inside it, aimed upward at prey silhouetted against the faint light above. The giant squid carries the largest eyes in the animal kingdom—the size of dinner plates—built, some think, to catch the small shadow of a sperm whale blotting out the glimmer of frightened plankton. Drifting among them are siphonophores, which are not individuals at all but colonies: dozens of cloned bodies, each specialized—one to swim, one to feed, one to sting—pretending, successfully, to be a single thing. And at the volcanic vents lives the scaly-foot snail, whose shell is armored with iron sulfide, an actual coat of metal, worn by a snail, at the bottom of the ocean, in perfect darkness.

When a great whale dies, it sinks, and its body becomes an island. Whole communities assemble on a single carcass, including the bone-eating worm *Osedax*, which has no mouth and no stomach and instead sends roots into whale bones, letting symbiotic bacteria digest the fat within. Some of these species live nowhere else on Earth, and one body can feed a community for decades. A death down there is not an ending so much as a slow banquet, outlasting many human careers.

The deepest trenches bear the name of Hades—the hadal zone—and their scale is planetary: Everest could slide into the Mariana Trench and leave two kilometers of water above its summit. Even there, life persists. Pale amphipods pick their way across the silt, and a soft, gelatinous, pinkish fish glides through the trench at depths nearing eight kilometers, unbothered by the weight of an ocean because it has never known anything else.

For most of the twentieth century, we assumed all life ran on sunlight—that photosynthesis sat at the base of everything. Then, in 1977, the submersible Alvin descended near the Galápagos and found volcanic vents crowned with tube worms taller than a person: animals with no mouth and no gut, farming bacteria inside them that feed on hydrogen sulfide—rotten-egg chemistry, sulfur and heat, instead of light. The textbooks were rewritten. Life, it turns out, does not require the sun, and some researchers now suspect it may have begun down there in the dark, eating the planet's own chemistry.

It is worth letting all of this rearrange the word *world*. The largest habitat on Earth is not the rainforest or the prairie; it is the deep sea—a country of night covering most of the planet, where most individuals of most species live and die without ever once being seen by us.

We point our telescopes at the stars and ask whether we are alone, and it is a good question. But we share this planet with a darkness we have barely introduced ourselves to, an alienness we can meet without crossing any light-years at all. Every submersible that switches on its floodlights down there is striking a match inside a cathedral no one has entered. The congregation glances up—lanternfish, squid, snails in iron shells—briefly lit, unimpressed, then returns to its blue, luminous business, as it has for ages upon ages, beneath the maps.
